{{Short description|Differential geometry term}}
{{For|twists of curves in algebraic geometry|twists of elliptic curves}}
In [[differential geometry]], the '''twist''' of a ''[[Ribbon (mathematics)|ribbon]]'' is its [[rate of change (mathematics)|rate]] of [[axial rotation]]. Let a ribbon <math>(X,U)</math> be composed of a [[space curve]], <math>X=X(s)</math>, where <math>s</math> is the [[arc length]] of <math>X</math>, and <math>U=U(s)</math> a unit [[normal vector]], perpendicular at each point to <math>{\partial X(s) \over \partial s}(s)</math>. Since the ribbon <math>(X,U)</math> has edges <math>X</math> and <math>X'=X+\varepsilon U</math>, the twist (or ''total twist number'') <math>Tw</math> measures the average [[winding number|winding]] of the edge curve <math>X'</math> around and along the axial curve <math>X</math>. According to Love (1944) twist is defined by

:<math> Tw = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \int \left( U \times \dfrac{dU}{ds} \right) \cdot \dfrac{dX}{ds} ds \; ,</math>

where <math>dX/ds</math> is the unit tangent vector to <math>X</math>.
The total twist number <math>Tw</math> can be decomposed (Moffatt & Ricca 1992) into ''normalized total torsion'' <math>T \in [0,1)</math> and ''intrinsic twist'' <math>N \in \mathbb{Z}</math> as

:<math> Tw = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \int \tau \; ds + \dfrac{\left[ \Theta \right]_X}{2\pi} = T+N \; ,</math>

where <math>\tau=\tau(s)</math> is the [[Torsion of a curve|torsion]] of the space curve <math>X</math>, and <math>\left[ \Theta \right]_X</math> denotes the total rotation angle of <math>U</math> along <math>X</math>.  Neither <math>N</math> nor <math>Tw</math> are independent of the ribbon field <math>U</math>.  Instead, only the normalized torsion <math>T</math> is an invariant of the curve <math>X</math> (Banchoff & White 1975).

When the ribbon is deformed so as to pass through an ''inflectional state'' (i.e. <math>X</math>  has a [[point of inflection]]), the torsion <math>\tau</math> becomes singular. The total torsion <math>T</math> jumps by <math>\pm 1</math> and the total angle <math>N</math> simultaneously makes an equal and opposite jump of <math> \mp 1 </math> (Moffatt & Ricca 1992) and <math>Tw</math> remains continuous. This behavior has many important consequences for energy considerations in many fields of science (Ricca 1997, 2005; Goriely 2006).

Together with the [[writhe]] <math>Wr</math> of <math>X</math>, twist is a geometric quantity that plays an important role in the application of the [[Călugăreanu–White–Fuller formula]] <math>Lk = Wr + Tw</math> in [[topological fluid dynamics]] (for its close relation to [[Hydrodynamical helicity|kinetic]] and [[magnetic helicity]] of a vector field), [[physical knot theory]], and [[Structural complexity (applied mathematics)|structural complexity]] analysis.
